title: The Jaffa Cake trial
hook: A British tax tribunal had to decide whether a Jaffa Cake is a cake or a biscuit.
peek: In 1991, McVitie's argued before a UK tax tribunal that its Jaffa Cakes were cakes, not biscuits. A lot of money rode on the answer, and one test the tribunal weighed was what happens to a Jaffa Cake when it goes stale.
lede: In Britain, most food carries no VAT, the sales tax. Chocolate-covered biscuits are an exception, while cakes, even chocolate-covered ones, are not taxed. That made the Jaffa Cake, a small sponge disc with orange jelly and a chocolate top, a puzzle worth arguing about. In 1991 McVitie's went to a VAT tribunal to argue it was a cake.

bullets.text: A key point: when a cake goes stale it turns hard, while a stale biscuit turns soft. Jaffa Cakes go hard, like cakes. McVitie's is also said to have baked a giant Jaffa Cake to show the tribunal what it really was.

The tribunal weighed several features. The name said cake. The batter of eggs, flour and sugar was a sponge cake batter. Against that, Jaffa Cakes are biscuit-sized, sold beside biscuits, and eaten with the fingers like one.
On balance, the tribunal ruled that Jaffa Cakes are cakes. McVitie's won, and Jaffa Cakes stayed free of VAT, saving the company and its customers a considerable sum.
McVitie's launched Jaffa Cakes in 1927, naming them after Jaffa oranges. The cake or biscuit question still splits British tea tables, but in law it has been settled since the ruling.
